Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe burning at Taberah.1–3The people lust for flesh, and loathe the manna.4–9Moses complains of his charge.10–15Elders appointed to divide the charge. Flesh meat promised.16–23The Spirit rests on the elders.24–30Quails are given.31–35
Fire breaks out at Taberah (verses 1–3)

The people complained.

This shows how sin can twist even something good into a reason for rebelling against God.

The law exposes sin but cannot conquer it.

Discontented people will always find something to complain about, however favorable their circumstances may be.

The Lord heard the murmuring, even when Moses did not.

He knows every secret resentment and complaint hidden in the heart.

God was displeased, and he sent a fire of judgment against the people.

They had allowed their anger against him to burn within them.

Now his just anger burned against their bodies.

Yet his judgment came gradually, leaving time for warning and repentance.

God does not delight in punishment.

Even after judgment begins, he is willing to stop when his people turn to him.

The people crave meat and reject manna (verses 4–9)

Human beings have lost their true place of rest and may remain dissatisfied even in prosperity.

Israel became tired of manna, though it was wholesome and nourishing food.

It cost nothing.

Gathering it took little labor.

Yet the people remembered the fish and other foods they had eaten in Egypt as though those meals had been free.

They forgot the crushing slavery through which they had paid for them.

While they ate manna, they were almost spared the burden of earning bread by the sweat of their faces.

Still they complained about God's provision.

A complaining spirit finds fault even with good gifts.

People who could be happy make themselves miserable through discontent.

They insisted they would not be satisfied unless they had meat.

A desire for bodily pleasure has become dangerous when it rules a person's choices.

We should not encourage any desire that we cannot sincerely turn into prayer.

Something lawful in itself may become sinful when God has not given it to us and we demand it out of uncontrolled appetite.

Moses complains under the burden of leadership (verses 10–15)

The people had provoked Moses terribly.

But his own response was not as fitting as it ought to have been.

He undervalued the honor God had given him.

He exaggerated the burden of his own work, even though divine wisdom guided him and almighty power could reward or correct the people.

His words showed distrust of God's grace.

If the work had been lighter, Moses could not have fulfilled it by his own strength.

If it had been heavier, he could still have done it through God's help.

Let us ask the Lord not to lead us into temptation.

Seventy elders are appointed; meat is promised (verses 16–23)

Moses was to choose people already recognized as wise and experienced elders.

God would equip them for the work.

If they were not already capable, he would make them capable.

God also promised meat to the discontented people, removing every excuse for further complaint.

Henry draws two lessons.

First, bodily pleasures are empty. They can overwhelm us through excess but cannot truly satisfy us.

Only spiritual pleasures satisfy and endure.

The world and its desires pass away.

Second, gluttony and drunkenness are degrading sins. They turn food and drink, which should nourish and strengthen the body, into causes of harm.

Moses questioned how God could provide such enormous quantities of meat.

Even great and genuine believers may find it difficult to trust God when visible circumstances seem hopeless.

God reminded Moses that the Lord is almighty.

He would soon see whether God's word came true.

When God speaks, he can accomplish what he promises.

The Spirit rests upon the elders (verses 24–30)

God fulfilled his promise to help Moses govern Israel.

He put his Spirit upon the seventy elders.

They spoke to the people about the things of God in a way that made his presence recognizable.

Two elders, Eldad and Medad, had not gone to the tabernacle.

Henry understands this as a sign that they felt unworthy and inadequate.

Nevertheless, the Holy Spirit met them in the camp, where they exercised gifts of prayer, preaching and praise.

The Spirit of God is not restricted to the tabernacle.

He moves where he wills, like the wind.

God exalts those who humble themselves.

People most capable of leadership are often those who are least ambitious for it.

Joshua wanted Eldad and Medad restrained.

He was not asking for punishment but feared their ministry might divide the people or rival Moses.

He acted out of concern for the unity of the community.

Moses, however, did not fear such consequences from the Spirit's genuine work.

We should not silence people whom Christ has acknowledged or prevent them from doing good simply because they disagree with us on some matters.

Moses longed for all God's people to become prophets and receive his Spirit.

Those seeking power should remember Moses' testimony: leadership is a burden.

It brings anxiety and responsibility to people who take their duty seriously.

For those who neglect it, the final accounting will be heavier still.

Leaders should welcome useful counsel and assistance rather than despising it.

If all God's people were enabled by Christ's Spirit to minister, there would still be enough work for everyone in calling sinners to repentance and faith, even if outward disagreements remained.

Quail are given and judgment follows (verses 31–35)

God gave Israel meat, as promised.

People are often much quicker to gather perishable food than to seek the food that lasts to eternal life.

We devote enormous energy to temporary advantages while neglecting our souls.

People ruled by fleshly desires may get exactly what they demand—even when fulfilling those desires ruins them.

Israel's feast proved costly.

God sometimes grants sinners' requests in judgment while denying his own people's desires in love.

What we crave improperly may become a source of grief and suffering if we obtain it.

Many people shorten their lives through excess.

Let us seek joys that truly satisfy, never sicken us through indulgence, and remain forever.

[Num.11.1-Num.11.3]
Chapter 11
Chapter Outline
The burning at Taberah. | (1-3) |
The people lust for flesh, and loathe the manna. | (4-9) |
Moses complains of his charge. | (10-15) |
Elders appointed to divide the charge. Flesh meat promised. | (16-23) |
The Spirit rests on the elders. | (24-30) |
Quails are given. | (31-35) |
Verses 1-3
Here is the people's sin; they complained. See the sinfulness of sin, which takes occasion from the commandment to be provoking. The weakness of the law discovered sin, but could not destroy it; checked, but could not conquer it. They complained. Those who are of a discontented spirit, will always find something to quarrel or fret about, though the circumstances of their outward condition be ever so favourable. The Lord heard it, though Moses did not. God knows the secret frettings and murmurings of the heart, though concealed from men. What he noticed, he was much displeased with, and he chastised them for this sin. The fire of their wrath against God burned in their minds; justly did the fire of God's wrath fasten on their bodies; but God's judgments came on them gradually, that they might take warning. It appeared that God delights not in punishing; when he begins, he is soon prevailed with to let it fall.
[Num.11.4-Num.11.9]
Verses 4-9
Man, having forsaken his proper rest, feels uneasy and wretched, though prosperous. They were weary of the provision God had made for them, although wholesome food and nourishing. It cost no money or care, and the labour of gathering it was very little indeed; yet they talked of Egypt's cheapness, and the fish they ate there freely; as if that cost them nothing, when they paid dearly for it with hard service! While they lived on manna, they seemed exempt from the curse sin has brought on man, that in the sweat of his face he should eat bread; yet they speak of it with scorn. Peevish, discontented minds will find fault with that which has no fault in it, but that it is too good for them. Those who might be happy, often make themselves miserable by discontent. They could not be satisfied unless they had flesh to eat. It is evidence of the dominion of the carnal mind, when we want to have the delights and satisfaction of sense. We should not indulge in any desire which we cannot in faith turn into prayer, as we cannot when we ask meat for our lust. What is lawful of itself becomes evil, when God does not allot it to us, yet we desire it.
[Num.11.10-Num.11.15]
Verses 10-15
The provocation was very great; yet Moses expressed himself otherwise than became him. He undervalued the honour God had put upon him. He magnified his own performances, while he had the Divine wisdom to direct him, and Almighty power to dispense rewards and punishments. He speaks distrustfully of the Divine grace. Had the work been much less he could not have gone through it in his own strength; but had it been much greater, through God strengthening him, he might have done it. Let us pray, Lord, lead us not into temptation.
[Num.11.16-Num.11.23]
Verses 16-23
Moses is to choose such as he knew to be elders, that is, wise and experienced men. God promises to qualify them. If they were not found fit for the employ, they should be made fit. Even the discontented people shall be gratified too, that every mouth may be stopped. See here, I. The vanity of all the delights of sense; they will cloy, but they will not satisfy. Spiritual pleasures alone will satisfy and last. As the world passes away, so do the lusts of it. 2. What brutish sins gluttony and drunkenness are! they make that to hurt the body which should be its health. Moses objects. Even true and great believers sometimes find it hard to trust God under the discouragements of second causes, and against hope to believe in hope. God here brings Moses to this point, The Lord God is Almighty; and puts the proof upon the issue, Thou shalt see whether my word shall come to pass or not. If he speaks, it is done.
[Num.11.24-Num.11.30]
Verses 24-30
We have here the fulfilment of God's word to Moses, that he should have help in the government of Israel. He gave of his Spirit to the seventy elders. They discoursed to the people of the things of God, so that all who heard them might say, that God was with them of a truth. Two of the elders, Eldad and Medad, went not out unto the tabernacle, as the rest, being sensible of their own weakness and unworthiness. But the Spirit of God found them in the camp, and there they exercised their gift of praying, preaching, and praising God; they spake as moved by the Holy Ghost. The Spirit of God is not confined to the tabernacle, but, like the wind, blows where He listeth. And they that humble themselves shall be exalted; and those who are most fit for government, are least ambitious of it. Joshua does not desire that they should be punished, but only restrained for the future. This motion he made out of zeal for what he thought to be the unity of the church. He would have them silenced, lest they should occasion a schism, or should rival Moses; but Moses was not afraid of any such effects from that Spirit which God had put upon them. Shall we reject those whom Christ has owned, or restrain any from doing good, because they are not in every thing of our mind? Moses wishes all the Lord's people were prophets, that he would put his Spirit upon all of them. Let the testimony of Moses be believed by those who desire to be in power; that government is a burden. It is a burden of care and trouble to those who make conscience of the duty of it; and to those who do not, it will prove a heavier burden in the day of account. Let the example of Moses be followed by those in power; let them not despise the advice and assistance of others, but desire it, and be thankful for it. If all the present number of the Lord's people were rendered prophets, or ministers, by the Spirit of Christ, though not all agreed in outward matters, there is work enough for all, in calling sinners to repentance, and faith in our Lord Jesus.
[Num.11.31-Num.11.35]
Verses 31-35
God performed his promise to the people, in giving them flesh. How much more diligent men are in collecting the meat that perishes, than in labouring for meat which endures to everlasting life! We are quick-sighted in the affairs of time; but stupidity blinds us as to the concerns of eternity. To pursue worldly advantages, we need no arguments; but when we are to secure the true riches, then we are all forgetfulness. Those who are under the power of a carnal mind, will have their lusts fulfilled, though it be to the certain damage and ruin of their precious souls. They paid dearly for their feasts. God often grants the desires of sinners in wrath, while he denies the desires of his own people in love. What we unduly desire, if we obtain it, we have reason to fear, will be some way or other a grief and cross to us. And what multitudes there are in all places, who shorten their lives by excess of one kind or other! Let us seek for those pleasures which satisfy, but never surfeit; and which will endure for evermore.

Miriam and Aaron criticize Moses (verses 1–9)

Moses' patience was tested by his own family as well as by the people he led.

Miriam and Aaron objected to his marriage to a foreign woman.

But Henry considers it probable that they were really motivated by wounded pride and envy of his greater authority.

Opposition from relatives and from friends who share our faith can hurt especially deeply.

We should expect such difficulties and seek to keep Moses' gentle and humble spirit.

These trials helped prepare Moses for his calling.

God not only defended Moses but praised him.

Moses was entrusted with prophetic revelation in a way that placed him above the other prophets.

Yet the least person in the kingdom of heaven enjoys a greater privilege, and Jesus Christ is infinitely greater than Moses (Hebrews 3:1).

Miriam and Aaron should have considered whom they were insulting.

We should be cautious about speaking against God's servants.

It is presumptuous to speak contemptuously about those in positions of dignity (2 Peter 2:10).

Nothing shows God's displeasure more sadly than his presence being withdrawn.

Woe to us if he leaves!

He does not withdraw until our sins and foolishness have driven him away.

Miriam is afflicted; Moses intercedes (verses 10–16)

The cloud departed, and Miriam was struck with leprosy.

When God's presence goes, distress follows.

Bishop Hall, whom Henry quotes, observed that her offensive tongue was punished by an afflicted appearance.

Aaron, as a priest, had to judge the condition.

He could not pronounce Miriam unclean without trembling, since he knew he was equally guilty.

If speaking against Moses was so serious, what will happen to those who sin against Christ?

Aaron, who had just criticized Moses with Miriam, now had to plead with him on behalf of both.

He was forced to speak respectfully of the very person he had blamed.

People who despise God's servants may one day need their help.

Correction has a good effect when it leads to confession and repentance.

Even offenders who are disciplined and publicly humbled may be forgiven.

Moses showed that he had forgiven the personal wrong done to him.

We should imitate his mercy and the Savior's prayer, “Father, forgive them.”

Miriam had to remain outside the camp for seven days, accepting the disgrace that followed her sin.

Whenever God corrects us, we should humbly acknowledge our wrongdoing.

Israel's journey was delayed by this event.

Many things can slow our progress, but nothing hinders our journey toward heaven more seriously than sin.
classic_reading:
[Num.12.1-Num.12.9]
Chapter 12
Chapter Outline
God rebukes the murmuring of Aaron and Miriam. | (1-9) |
Miriam struck with leprosy, and healed at the prayer of Moses. | (10-16) |
Verses 1-9
The patience of Moses was tried in his own family, as well as by the people. The pretence was, that he had married a foreign wife; but probably their pride was hurt, and their envy stirred up, by his superior authority. Opposition from our near relations, and from religious friends, is most painful. But this is to be looked for, and it will be well if in such circumstances we can preserve the gentleness and meekness of Moses. Moses was thus fitted to the work he was called to. God not only cleared Moses, but praised him. Moses had the spirit of prophecy in a way which set him far above all other prophets; yet he that is least in the kingdom of heaven, is greater than he; and our Lord Jesus infinitely excels him, [Heb.3.1] He 3:1. Let Miriam and Aaron consider whom it was they insulted. We have reason to be afraid of saying or doing any thing against the servants of God. And those are presumptuous indeed who are not afraid to speak evil of dignities, [2Pet.2.10] 2Pe 2:10. The removal of God's presence is the surest and saddest token of God's displeasure. Woe to us, if he depart! he never departs, till by sin and folly we drive him from us.
[Num.12.10-Num.12.16]
Verses 10-16
The cloud departed, and Miriam became leprous. When God goes, evil comes: expect no good when God departs. Her foul tongue, as Bishop Hall says, was justly punished with a foul face. Aaron, as priest, was judge of the leprosy. He could not pronounce her leprous without trembling, knowing himself to be equally guilty. But if she was thus punished for speaking against Moses, what will become of those who sin against Christ? Aaron, who joined his sister in speaking against Moses, is forced for himself and his sister, to beseech him, and to speak highly of him whom he had so lately blamed. Those who trample upon the saints and servants of God, will one day be glad to make court to them. It is well when rebukes produce confession of sin and repentance. Such offenders, though corrected and disgraced, shall be pardoned. Moses made it appear, that he forgave the injury done him. To this pattern of Moses, and that of our Saviour, who said, "Father, forgive them," we must conform. A reason is given for Miriam's being put out of the camp for seven days; because thus she ought to accept the punishment of her sin. When under the tokens of God's displeasure for sin, it becomes us to take shame to ourselves. This hindered the people's progress in their march forward towards Canaan. Many things oppose us, but nothing so hinders us in the way to heaven, as sin.

Twelve spies are sent to Canaan (verses 1–20)

This chapter begins the sad account, continued in the next chapter, of Israel turning back at the borders of Canaan.

Because of unbelief and complaining, that generation would be sentenced to wander and die in the wilderness.

According to Deuteronomy 1:22, the proposal to send scouts came from the people.

They trusted their own strategy more than God's wisdom.

This is how we harm ourselves when we trust what our senses report rather than what God has revealed.

We walk by sight rather than by faith.

Moses told the twelve men to be courageous.

Their task was difficult and required good judgment and determination.

But it was also a great responsibility requiring faithfulness.

True courage in such circumstances grows from strong faith.

Only Caleb and Joshua possessed that faith.

The spies explore the land (verses 21–25)

The scouts brought back a large cluster of grapes and other fruit.

These gave evidence of the land's goodness.

They were a sample and a promise of the harvest Israel could later enjoy in Canaan.

Likewise, the comfort we now receive through fellowship with God gives us a foretaste of the complete joy awaiting us in the heavenly Canaan.

From those present blessings, we gain some idea of what heaven will be like.

The spies give their report (verses 26–33)

It is astonishing that Israel waited forty days for the scouts' return when the people were already at the border, prepared to enter the land.

They had received every assurance that God's power and promise would bring success.

His earlier miracles should have confirmed that assurance.

Yet they distrusted both him and his word.

How much harm we bring upon ourselves through unbelief!

When the scouts returned, most of them discouraged the people.

Israel had depended upon human judgments when God's own promise was sufficient.

It was therefore just that the people's misplaced confidence brought this severe temptation upon them.

The land was as good as God had said.

But the scouts refused to believe that possessing it was as certain as he had promised.

They looked at military difficulties and despaired of receiving what the God of truth had guaranteed.

Caleb, supported only by Joshua, urged Israel to go forward.

He did not say, “Let us go conquer it,” but “Let us go possess it.”

Faith took hold of God's promise instead of relying on human power.

The difficulties in salvation become small when we exercise living, active faith in God's strength and promises.

Whatever God has truly promised is possible for those who believe.

We cannot trust merely worldly reasoning or people who profess faith while depending on sight.

Unbelief forgets God's power, magnifies dangers and fills the heart with fear.

May the Lord help us believe him and discover that his promise is certain.
classic_reading:
[Num.13.1-Num.13.20]
Chapter 13
Chapter Outline
Twelve men sent to search the land of Canaan, Their instructions. | (1-20) |
Their proceedings. | (21-25) |
Their account of the land. | (26-33) |
Verses 1-20
A memorable and melancholy history is related in this and the following chapter, of the turning back of Israel from the borders of Canaan, and the sentencing them to wander and perish in the wilderness, for their unbelief and murmuring. It appears, [Deut.1.22] De 1:22, that the motion to search out the land came from the people. They had a better opinion of their own policy than of God's wisdom. Thus we ruin ourselves by believing the reports and representations of sense rather than Divine revelation. We walk by sight not by faith. Moses gave the spies this charge, Be of good courage. It was not only a great undertaking they were put upon, which required good management and resolution; but a great trust was reposed in them, which required that they should be faithful. Courage in such circumstances can only spring from strong faith, which Caleb and Joshua alone possessed.
[Num.13.21-Num.13.25]
Verses 21-25
The searchers of the land brought a bunch of grapes with them, and other fruits, as proofs of the goodness of the country; which was to Israel both the earnest and the specimen of all the fruits of Canaan. Such are the present comforts we have in communion with God, foretastes of the fulness of joy we expect in the heavenly Canaan. We may see by them what heaven is.
[Num.13.26-Num.13.33]
Verses 26-33
We may wonder that the people of Israel staid forty days for the return of their spies, when they were ready to enter Canaan, under all the assurances of success they could have from the Divine power, and the miracles that had hitherto attended them. But they distrusted God's power and promise. How much we stand in our own light by our unbelief! At length the messengers returned; but the greater part discouraged the people from going forward to Canaan. Justly are the Israelites left to this temptation, for putting confidence in the judgment of men, when they had the word of God to trust in. Though they had found the land as good as God had said, yet they would not believe it to be as sure as he had said, but despaired of having it, though Eternal Truth had engaged it to them. This was the representation of the evil spies. Caleb, however, encouraged them to go forward, though seconded by Joshua only. He does not say, Let us go up and conquer it; but, Let us go and possess it. Difficulties that are in the way of salvation, dwindle and vanish before a lively, active faith in the power and promise of God. All things are possible, if they are promised, to him that believes; but carnal sense and carnal professors are not to be trusted. Unbelief overlooks the promises and power of God, magnifies every danger and difficulty, and fills the heart with discouragement. May the Lord help us to believe! we shall then find all things possible.

The people refuse to trust God's promise (verses 1–4)

People who refuse to trust God continually trouble themselves.

The grief produced by worldly unbelief brings death.

Israel complained against Moses and Aaron, but in criticizing them the people were really rebuking the Lord.

They looked back at Egypt with unreasonable discontent.

Uncontrolled fear and anger can make people foolishly throw away even what they ought to treasure most: life itself.

They said they would rather die as guilty people under God's judgment than live as victorious people enjoying his favor.

Finally, they decided to return to Egypt rather than enter Canaan.

People who abandon God's counsel are choosing their own ruin.

Could Israel expect the cloud to guide them back or manna to accompany them?

Even if entering Canaan were as difficult as they feared, returning to Egypt would have been harder.

We often complain about our circumstances and wish to change them.

But there is no place or condition on earth where a determinedly dissatisfied person cannot find something to resent.

The better way to improve our situation is to cultivate a better spirit.

Turning from God leads inevitably toward disaster.

Joshua and Caleb urge the people to trust (verses 5–10)

Moses and Aaron were astonished that Israel could throw away its greatest blessings.

Joshua and Caleb assured the people that Canaan was good and worth entering.

They did not treat its conquest as an impossible problem.

If people understood how desirable the blessings of faith are, they would not shrink from the duties that come with it.

The Canaanites lived in strongly fortified towns, but their protection had departed from them.

The other scouts noticed the Canaanites' military power.

Joshua and Caleb recognized the Canaanites' wickedness and the judgment awaiting them.

No people can remain safe after provoking God to abandon them.

Though Israel lived in tents, God's presence was its defense.

With him, the most powerful enemy need not terrify us.

Sinners bring ruin on themselves through rebellion.

But people who, like Caleb and Joshua, stand faithfully for God may trust his special protection.

He will shelter them from human hostility either during this life or in heaven.

Moses intercedes after God's warning (<reference osisRef="Num.14.11-Num.14.19" resp="BibleResourcesOriginalSourceRangeInModernSectionHeading">verses 11–19</reference>)

Moses humbly prayed for Israel.

In this he pictured Jesus Christ, who prayed for those who treated him cruelly.

The pardon Moses sought was the removal of the nation's threatened punishment.

He pleaded earnestly that God's abundant mercy was consistent with forgiving them.

The unbelieving generation is excluded (verses 20–35)

The Lord answered Moses' prayer by not destroying the entire congregation immediately.

Yet refusal to believe God's promise excluded that generation from enjoying its fulfillment.

Those who despised the pleasant land would not enter it.

God would keep his promise to their children.

The people had said they would rather die in the wilderness.

Their sin became their ruin: God allowed their own words to be fulfilled, and their bodies fell in the desert.

They suffered under the heavy burden of their own wrongdoing.

The expression about God's broken promise indicated both the cause and the consequence of their loss.

The cause was their unbelief: God does not abandon people until they have first turned from him.

The consequence was their destruction.

But the children younger than twenty—whom their parents had feared would be captured—would be brought safely into Canaan.

In this way God distinguished between guilty adults and their children, judging the former without destroying the latter.

He did not utterly remove his covenant kindness.

The faithless spies die (verses 36–39)

The ten spies who had brought an evil report about Canaan died suddenly.

They had slandered the land God promised.

People provoke God severely when they misrepresent true religion or make others dislike it.

The complainers now became mourners.

Had they grieved over their sin while they were being warned, the sentence might have been prevented.

But their sorrow was chiefly over the punishment, so it did not help them.

There is a similar grief in hell, where tears cannot end the fire or relieve the suffering.

Israel attacks without God's blessing (verses 40–45)

Some Israelites now became eager to march into Canaan.

But the right time had passed.

How much better it would be if people sought heaven earnestly while the time for receiving God's grace remains, instead of waiting until it is too late!

An action that was our duty at the proper time may become sinful when done in defiance of God's later command.

People who abandon their duty cannot claim God's protection.

Israel refused to move when the Lord commanded it, then insisted on moving when he forbade it.

This is the hostility of a sinful mind against God.

Earlier the people distrusted God's power.

Now they presumed upon their own strength without him.

Their expedition therefore failed.

The judgment that their bodies would fall in the wilderness had begun.

Nothing founded upon sin can end well.

To enjoy peace with friends and success against enemies, we need the Lord's friendship and must remain in his love.

Let Israel's history warn us against dying through the same unbelief.

Let us go forward trusting God's mercy, power, promise and truth, confident that he will bring our souls to everlasting rest.
classic_reading:
[Num.14.1-Num.14.4]
Chapter 14
Chapter Outline
The people murmur at the account of the spies. | (1-4) |
Joshua and Caleb labour to still the people. | (5-10) |
The Divine threatenings, The intercession of Moses. | (11-19) |
The murmurers forbidden to enter the promised land. | (20-35) |
Death of the evil spies. | (36-39) |
Defeat of the people, who now would invade the land. | (40-45) |
Verses 1-4
Those who do not trust God, continually vex themselves. The sorrow of the world worketh death. The Israelites murmured against Moses and Aaron, and in them reproached the Lord. They look back with causeless discontent. See the madness of unbridled passions, which makes men prodigal of what nature accounts most dear, life itself. They wish rather to die criminals under God's justice, than to live conquerors in his favour. At last they resolve, that, instead of going forward to Canaan, they would go back to Egypt. Those who walk not in God's counsels, seek their own ruin. Could they expect that God's cloud would lead them, or his manna attend them? Suppose the difficulties of conquering Canaan were as they imagined, those of returning to Egypt were much greater. We complain of our place and lot, and we would change; but is there any place or condition in this world, that has not something in it to make us uneasy, if we are disposed to be so? The way to better our condition, is to get our spirits in a better frame. See the folly of turning from the ways of God. But men run on the certain fatal consequences of a sinful course.
[Num.14.5-Num.14.10]
Verses 5-10
Moses and Aaron were astonished to see a people throw away their own mercies. Caleb and Joshua assured the people of the goodness of the land. They made nothing of the difficulties in the way of their gaining it. If men were convinced of the desirableness of the gains of religion, they would not stick at the services of it. Though the Canaanites dwell in walled cities, their defence was departed from them. The other spies took notice of their strength, but these of their wickedness. No people can be safe, when they have provoked God to leave them. Though Israel dwell in tents, they are fortified. While we have the presence of God with us, we need not fear the most powerful force against us. Sinners are ruined by their own rebellion. But those who, like Caleb and Joshua, faithfully expose themselves for God, are sure to be taken under his special protection, and shall be hid from the rage of men, either under heaven or in heaven. ( [Num.14.11-Num.14.19] Nu 14:11-19)

Moses made humble intercession for Israel. Herein he was a type of Christ, who prayed for those that despitefully used him. The promise of God should be fulfilled to their children. They wished to die in the wilderness; God made their sin their ruin, took them at their word, and their carcases fell in the wilderness. They were made to groan under the burden of their own sin, which was too heavy for them to bear. Grain and drink offerings; one law for foreigners (verses 1–21)

God gave detailed instructions about the grain and drink offerings accompanying sacrifices.

The opening words were encouraging: when Israel came into the land that the Lord would give them.

This assured the people that the promised land would still be given to their descendants.

Because the offerings were considered the food of God's table, bread, oil and wine were to accompany the sacrifices of animals.

These rules fixed the appropriate proportions for each kind of offering.

They applied equally to native Israelites and foreigners living among them.

That equality anticipated the calling of the Gentiles and their acceptance into God's church.

If the Mosaic law made so little distinction between Jew and Gentile in these matters, the gospel breaks down the dividing wall even more completely and reconciles both to God.

Offerings for sins committed unknowingly (verses 22–29)

Ignorance may lessen a person's guilt in some respects, but it cannot justify people who could have learned God's will and failed to do so.

David prayed to be cleansed from his hidden faults, including sins he had not recognized.

Sins committed through ignorance can be forgiven through Christ, the great Sacrifice.

When he offered himself once for all on the cross, he prayed, “Father, forgive them; they do not know what they are doing.”

That prayer revealed part of the saving purpose of his offering.

It is also a gracious sign of God's favor toward Gentiles that the law explicitly included foreigners among those who could receive atonement for unintended sins.

Deliberate sin and the Sabbath-breaker (verses 30–36)

People sin presumptuously when they deliberately act against God's known will and glory.

Such sins are especially evil.

The deliberate offender insults the Lord and despises his word.

Presumptuous sinners behave as though they are too important, too good or too wise to accept its rule.

The account of the Sabbath-breaker is a particular example.

He gathered wood on the Sabbath to make a fire, though the people had been instructed to prepare their baking and cooking the previous day (Exodus 16:23).

His action was therefore a deliberate affront to both God's law and the One who gave it.

God is jealous for the honor of his Sabbath.

He will not overlook its contemptuous profanation, whatever people may do.

Henry sees the severe penalty under Israel's law as a warning that God's judgments are consistent with perfect justice and love.

God has a right to a day devoted to himself.

People deny that right when they listen to their pride and unbelief rather than to the Spirit of truth.

Henry then challenges Christians who turn their backs on the blessings of Sabbath worship in order to accumulate wealth or pursue sinful pleasures.

They may gain money or excitement, but they will also receive the dreadful consequences of their disobedience.

Sinful pursuits finally lead to ruin.

Tassels as reminders of God's commands (verses 37–41)

The Lord instructed Israel to put fringes or tassels on the borders of their clothes.

Their dress, like their diet, would distinguish them from surrounding nations.

They were taught not to conform to the pagan ways of those nations in other matters.

Wherever they went, they visibly acknowledged that they belonged to God and were not ashamed of his law.

The fringes were not intended mainly as decoration.

Their purpose was to stir memory and attention (2 Peter 3:1).

When temptation came, seeing them should remind an Israelite not to break God's commandments.

We should likewise use every good means to keep Scripture's truth and commands in our thoughts.

Such reminders strengthen obedience and prepare the mind to resist temptation.

We are to be holy to our God: cleansed from sin and sincerely devoted to his service.

The repeated reason for every command remains the same: he is the Lord our God.

David prayed to be cleansed from his secret faults, those sins which he himself was not aware of. Sins committed ignorantly, shall be forgiven through Christ the great Sacrifice, who, when he offered up himself once for all upon the cross, seemed to explain one part of the intention of his offering, in that prayer, Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do. [Num.15.30-Num.15.36]
Verses 30-36
Those are to be reckoned presumptuous sinners, who sin designedly against God's will and glory. Sins thus committed are exceedingly sinful. He that thus breaks the commandment reproaches the Lord. He also despises the word of the Lord. Presumptuous sinners despise it, thinking themselves too great, too good, and too wise, to be ruled by it. A particular instance of presumption in the sin of sabbath-breaking is related. The offence was gathering sticks on the sabbath day, to make a fire, whereas the people were to bake and seethe what they had occasion for, the day before, [Exod.16.23] Ex 16:23. This was done as an affront both to the law and to the Lawgiver. God is jealous for the honour of his sabbaths, and will not hold him guiltless who profanes them, whatever men may do. God intended this punishment for a warning to all, to make conscience of keeping holy the sabbath. And we may be assured that no command was ever given for the punishment of sin, which, at the judgment day, shall not prove to have come from perfect love and justice. Wherein consists the difference between him who was detected gathering sticks in the wilderness on the day of God, and the man who turns his back upon the blessings of sabbath appointments, and the promises of sabbath mercies, to use his time, his cares, and his soul, in heaping up riches; and waste his hours, his property, and his strength in sinful pleasure? The people are ordered by the Lord to make fringes on the borders of their garments. They proclaimed themselves Jews wherever they were, as not ashamed of God and his law. The fringes were not appointed for trimming and adorning their clothes, but to stir up their minds by way of remembrance, [2Pet.3.1] 2Pe 3:1. If they were tempted to sin, the fringe would warn them not to break God's commandments. We should use every means of refreshing our memories with the truths and precepts of God's word, to strengthen and quicken our obedience, and arm our minds against temptation. Be holy unto your God; cleansed from sin, and sincerely devoted to his service; and that great reason for all the commandments is again and again repeated, "I am the Lord your God."

Korah's rebellion against the priesthood (verses 1–11)

Pride and ambition cause much harm both within churches and in nations.

Korah's company challenged God's appointment of Aaron and his family to the priesthood.

They claimed that the whole congregation was holy and favored by God.

But Israel had repeatedly defiled itself through sin and was still living under signs of God's displeasure.

The rebels falsely accused Moses and Aaron of claiming special honor for themselves, when in fact God had called them to their offices.

Henry identifies their attitude as the spirit of people who refuse to accept the authority God has established over them.

He also reflects on the harsh treatment that faithful servants may receive after serving others.

Moses did not immediately retaliate.

He sought guidance from God, as wise people should do when considering how to answer difficult accusations.

He reminded the rebels of the privileges they already enjoyed as Levites.

They were despising gifts from God because they wanted the office he had given someone else.

One way to resist envy of those above us is to consider how many people have fewer opportunities than we do.

Dathan and Abiram refuse to obey (verses 12–15)

Moses summoned Dathan and Abiram to hear their complaints.

They refused to come.

They made thoroughly false accusations against him.

The people most deserving of honor are sometimes condemned most bitterly.

Moses was a remarkably gentle man, but he became deeply angry when God's honor was attacked through him.

He could not bear to see the people driving themselves toward ruin.

He appealed to God to bear witness to his integrity.

The rebels were ordered to appear with Aaron the following morning, when the morning incense would be offered.

Korah agreed.

Proud and ambitious people often arrange their own humiliation while imagining they are securing advancement.

God's glory appears; Moses and Aaron plead for the people (verses 16–22)

The same divine glory that had appeared when Aaron was first installed in his office (Leviticus 9:23) now appeared to confirm his calling and defeat his opponents.

Few things are more terrifying to a guilty conscience than the visible glory of God.

It is dangerous to associate closely with people engaged in serious rebellion and to join in their wrongdoing.

Although the Israelites had betrayed Moses and Aaron, the two men continued acting as faithful shepherds of the nation.

Someone else's failure to do right by us never cancels our obligation to seek that person's good.

Their earnest prayer was heard.

The earth opens beneath the rebels (verses 23–34)

The seventy elders accompanied Moses.

We should do what is right to support lawful authority when it is under unjust attack.

Anyone who wants to avoid sharing a sinner's destruction must separate from that person's evil conduct.

In response to Moses' prayer, God moved the congregation to withdraw from the rebels for safety.

The grace that leads people to separate from evil accompanies salvation.

God left the rebels to their own stubbornness and hard hearts.

Under divine instruction, Moses declared that if these men died ordinarily, he would accept being judged a fraud.

Immediately after he spoke, God opened the ground and swallowed up the rebels.

Their children also perished.

Henry admits that we cannot know all that might justify God's judgment of them, or all the mercy God might otherwise show them; but he maintains that infinite justice cannot do wrong.

The event was wholly miraculous.

God can appoint extraordinary judgments for people who persist in evil.

The earth is still burdened with human wrongdoing; Henry marvels that it does not sink beneath the weight.

The destruction of others should warn us.

If we could hear by faith the cries of those lost under judgment, we would be more diligent about escaping the same condemnation.

Fire consumes those offering unauthorized incense (verses 35–40)

Fire came from the Lord and consumed the 250 men who were offering incense.

Aaron remained alive among them.

God guards the honor of the worship he has appointed.

He will not allow people to seize offices and religious privileges he has not given them.

The sacrifice of the wicked is offensive to him.

The censers used by the rebels were set apart and then turned into a covering for the altar, so that even those objects would serve God's glory.

The covering reminded future Israelites of this judgment, warning them not to rebel in the same presumptuous way.

The rebels had brought destruction on themselves.

Likewise, those who break God's law and neglect his gospel choose the path of death.

The earth had scarcely closed over the rebels when the people began complaining again.

They had ignored all the warnings.

They even called the condemned rebels God's people and accused divine justice of wrongdoing.

Their stubbornness, after both Sinai's awe-inspiring law and severe judgments, showed how necessary God's grace is to change human hearts.

Love can accomplish what fear alone cannot.

Moses and Aaron again pleaded for mercy.

They understood the seriousness of the people's rebellion.

Aaron hurried with incense and stood between the living and the dead.

He did not burn incense to purify the air.

He was pleading that God's offended justice would be satisfied and the plague stopped.

Because he cared about every Israelite's life, he went as quickly as possible.

We are called to repay evil with good.

Aaron here pictured Christ.

The world suffers from the deadly infection of sin.

Only Jesus Christ's cross and intercession can remove it.

He entered the defiled and dying camp of humanity.

He stood between the Judge and those condemned by sin.

Through his blood we receive redemption and forgiveness.

If we admire Aaron's willingness, how much more should we praise the Savior's love in taking our place and purchasing us with his life!

God showed his love while we were still sinners: Christ died for us (Romans 5:8).

Moses summoned Dathan and Abiram to bring their complaints; but they would not obey. They bring very false charges against Moses. Those often fall under the heaviest censures, who in truth deserve the highest praise. Moses, though the meekest man, yet, finding God reproached in him, was very wroth; he could not bear to see the people ruining themselves. He appeals to God as to his own integrity. He bade them appear with Aaron next morning, at the time of offering the morning incense. Korah undertook thus to appear. Proud ambitious men, while projecting their own advancement, often hurry on their own shameful fall.
[Num.16.16-Num.16.22]
Verses 16-22
The same glory of the Lord that appeared to place Aaron in his office at first, [Lev.9.23] Le 9:23, now appeared to confirm him in it; and to confound those who set up against him. Nothing is more terrible to those who are conscious of guilt, than the appearance of the Divine glory. See how dangerous it is to have fellowship with sinners, and to partake with them. Though the people had treacherously deserted them, yet Moses and Aaron approved themselves faithful shepherds of Israel. If others fail in their duty to us, that does not take away the obligations we are under to seek their welfare. Their prayer was a pleading prayer, and it proved a prevailing one.
[Num.16.23-Num.16.34]
Verses 23-34
The seventy elders of Israel attend Moses. It is our duty to do what we can to countenance and support lawful authority when it is opposed. And those who would not perish with sinners, must come out from among them, and be separate. It was in answer to the prayer of Moses, that God stirred up the hearts of the congregation to remove for their own safety. Grace to separate from evil-doers is one of the things that accompany salvation. God, in justice, left the rebels to the obstinacy and hardness of their own hearts. Moses, by Divine direction, when all Israel were waiting the event, declares that if the rebels die a common death, he will be content to be called and counted an imposter. As soon as Moses had spoken the word, God caused the earth to open and swallow them all up. The children perished with their parents; in which, though we cannot tell how bad they might be to deserve it, or how good God might be otherwise to them; yet of this we are sure, that Infinite Justice did them no wrong. It was altogether miraculous. God has, when he pleases, strange punishments for the workers of iniquity. It was very significant. Considering how the earth is still in like manner loaded with the weight of man's sins, we have reason to wonder that it does not now sink under its load. The ruin of others should be our warning. Could we, by faith, hear the outcries of those that are gone down to the bottomless pit, we should give more diligence than we do to escape for our lives, lest we also come into their condemnation.

The censers are devoted, and, as all devoted things, must be made serviceable to the glory of God. This covering of the altar would remind the children of Israel of this event, that others might hear and fear, and do no more presumptuously. They brought destruction on themselves both in body and soul. Thus all who break the law and neglect the gospel choose and love death.

The gaping earth was scarcely closed, before the same sins are again committed, and all these warnings slighted. They called the rebels the people of the Lord; and find fault with Divine justice. God had already performed several miracles to punish Israel's sin.

Now, in his grace, he performed another miracle to prevent further sin.

Twelve staffs were brought before the Lord.

Henry considers it likely that these were old, dry staffs carried by the tribal leaders as signs of their authority.

Fruitfulness is among the best signs of a divine calling.

What God plants will flourish.

Yet they were still resisting God's judgments rather than accepting responsibility for their own pride and stubbornness.

It is wicked to complain against God during suffering in a way that brings still more sin.

If we perish through our rebellion, the guilt is ours.

God's judgment will prevail.

Even the most stubborn opponents will eventually be forced to recognize their folly.

How great are the mercies offered to us through a clearer and better covenant, founded on better promises!

This was the language of a repining people, quarrelling with the judgments of God, which by their own pride and obstinacy they brought upon themselves. It is very wicked to fret against God when we are in affliction, and in our distress thus to trespass yet more. If we die, if we perish, it is of ourselves, and the blame will be upon our own heads. When God judges, he will overcome, and will oblige the most obstinate gainsayers to confess their folly. And how great are our mercies, that we have a clearer and a better dispensation, established upon better promises!

The responsibilities of priests and Levites (verses 1–7)

The Israelites complained that approaching God was difficult and dangerous.

God therefore reminded them that the priests were appointed to come near to him on their behalf.

Aaron had no reason to be proud of his promotion.

His office carried heavy responsibilities and serious risks.

People entrusted with great authority or important work should remain humble and reverent toward God.

The greater the trust placed in us, the more danger there is that we might betray it.

This is one reason not to envy another person's honors or seek a high position merely for status.

God's provision for the priests (verses 8–19)

All believers are spiritual priests, and God has promised to care for them.

Faithfulness to him carries promises for this life as well as the next.

From the provision made for Israel's priests, the apostle teaches that Christian congregations should support their ministers.

Poor or inadequate support can contribute to ministers' falling into disgraceful behavior.

Priests were to devote themselves fully to their sacred work.

They were not to be constantly distracted or disturbed by worries about earning a living through ordinary business.

Their lives should also demonstrate faith in God's providence and in the worship he had appointed.

The finest portions of firstfruits were to be offered to the Lord.

Those who try to save for themselves by giving God only unwanted leftovers deceive themselves.

God is not mocked.

God's provision for the Levites (verses 20–32)

Just as Israel was distinct from other nations, the Levites were distinct from the other tribes.

People who have God himself as their permanent inheritance and portion should regard the world's possessions with a holy freedom from attachment.

The Levites also had to give God his due from their tithes, just as the other Israelites gave from their harvests.

Henry draws two lessons from verse 31 about enjoying earthly possessions without guilt.

First, what we own must have been obtained honestly and through rightful work.

Food is best enjoyed when earned through labor.

Anyone unwilling to work should not expect to eat (2 Thessalonians 3:10).

Second, God must receive the portion due to him.

We can enjoy our possessions properly when we have honored the Lord through them.

Giving the best to him prevents our possessions from becoming occasions of sin.

We should also give generously to those in need, so that what remains is enjoyed gratefully and with a clear conscience.

The ashes of the red heifer (verses 1–10)

The heifer was to be burned completely.

Henry sees this as a picture of Jesus Christ enduring great suffering in body and soul when he offered himself as a sacrifice.

By bearing God's just anger against human sin, Christ made atonement.

The ashes were preserved for ceremonial purification.

They could not themselves wash away moral guilt.

But they pointed toward the true cleansing of sin accomplished by our Lord's death.

The benefits of Christ's blood are set before us through God's word and the sacraments.

They are like a continuing fountain of saving merit to which believers may come by faith, again and again, for the cleansing of their consciences.

Cleansing people made unclean through death (verses 11–22)

Why did touching a dead body produce ceremonial uncleanness?

Because death is the wages of sin.

Sin brought death into the world, and death continues to reign through sin's power.

The Mosaic law could not conquer death or abolish it.

But the gospel reveals life and immortality and opens the way to a better hope.

The ashes of the heifer represented Christ's saving merit.

The flowing water represented the power and grace of the Holy Spirit, whom Scripture compares to rivers of living water.

The Spirit applies Christ's righteousness to us, bringing genuine cleansing.

People who expect to benefit from Christ's righteousness while refusing the Spirit's sanctifying influence are deceiving themselves.

The ashes did not accomplish their purpose without water.

Likewise, Christ's saving work is not to be separated from the Spirit's transforming work.

Without their connection to Christ's sacrifice, these regulations would be difficult to understand.

Reading them alongside the New Testament makes their spiritual meaning clear.

They reveal the fallen human condition and the defiling power of sin.

They also warn us to keep away from evil influences and corrupting companionship.

Verses 1-10
The heifer was to be wholly burned. This typified the painful sufferings of our Lord Jesus, both in soul and body, as a sacrifice made by fire, to satisfy God's justice for man's sin. These ashes are said to be laid up as a purification for sin, because, though they were only to purify from ceremonial uncleanness, yet they were a type of that purification for sin which our Lord Jesus made by his death. The blood of Christ is laid up for us in the word and sacraments, as a fountain of merit, to which by faith we may have constant recourse, for cleansing our consciences.
[Num.19.11-Num.19.22]
Verses 11-22
Why did the law make a corpse a defiling thing? Because death is the wages of sin, which entered into the world by it, and reigns by the power of it. The law could not conquer death, nor abolish it, as the gospel does, by bringing life and immortality to light, and so introducing a better hope. As the ashes of the heifer signified the merit of Christ, so the running water signified the power and grace of the blessed Spirit, who is compared to rivers of living water; and it is by his work that the righteousness of Christ is applied to us for our cleansing. Those who promise themselves benefit by the righteousness of Christ, while they submit not to the grace and influence of the Holy Spirit, do but deceive themselves; we cannot be purified by the ashes, otherwise than in the running water. What use could there be in these appointments, if they do not refer to the doctrines concerning the sacrifice of Christ? But comparing them with the New Testament, the knowledge to be got from them is evident. The true state of fallen man is shown in these institutions. Here we learn the defiling nature of sin, and are warned to avoid evil communications.

Israel complains again; Moses and Aaron fail (verses 1–13)

After thirty-eight weary years in the wilderness, Israel began moving toward Canaan once more.

There was no water for the congregation.

We live in a world full of needs.

Wherever we go, we should expect something to disturb our comfort.

Having abundant water is a great mercy. If we lacked it, we would value it more.

The people complained against Moses and Aaron.

They spoke the same unreasonable and bitter words their parents had spoken.

Their conduct was especially blameworthy because their families had suffered for years as a result of the earlier generation's complaining and unbelief.

Yet they repeated the very same sins.

God directed Moses to bring water from a rock again.

The Lord was no less able to supply his people than before.

But Moses and Aaron sinned in the way they handled the miracle.

They spoke as though the power belonged partly to themselves.

“Must we bring you water?”

That took some of the glory that belonged to God alone.

They were commanded to speak to the rock.

Instead, Moses struck it.

In this way they failed to honor the Lord as holy and failed to give him the complete glory he deserved.

Provoked by the people, Moses also spoke rashly.

Henry sees in this the continuing sinful desire of people to take over the work of the one appointed Mediator.

We try to become our own wisdom, righteousness, holiness and redemption.

But the gospel condemns every attempt to live independently of the Savior.

Edom refuses Israel passage (verses 14–21)

The shortest route to Canaan passed through Edom.

Moses sent messengers asking permission to travel through the country.

The Edomites refused.

They feared that Israel's large army might cause them harm.

Such fears might have been understandable if Israel were not under the discipline of the righteous God himself.

But Edom's hostility also continued the hatred that Esau had shown Jacob because of the blessing.

Now the old resentment reappeared as Jacob's descendants approached their inheritance.

We should not be surprised when unreasonable people reject fair requests or when people favored by God are treated with contempt.

Aaron dies and Eleazar becomes priest (verses 22–29)

God told Aaron to prepare for death.

The command expressed both displeasure and mercy.

There was displeasure because Aaron could not enter Canaan after his failure at the waters of Meribah.

But there was mercy because he was allowed to die peacefully, with honor, as someone received into the care of divine grace.

His exclusion from Canaan also had spiritual meaning.

It showed that the Levitical priesthood could not make anything perfect.

A better hope had to be introduced.

Aaron submitted to the appointed manner and time of his death.

As far as the record shows, he did so as peacefully as someone preparing to sleep.

He could see his beloved son Eleazar succeed him.

The priesthood would continue.

Even more importantly, that succession pointed toward the eternal priesthood of Christ.

A good person should want to remain useful for as long as God wills.

Why should we desire to stay in this world beyond the time when we can serve the Lord and our generation?

Verses 1-13
After thirty-eight years' tedious abode in the wilderness, the armies of Israel advanced towards Canaan again. There was no water for the congregation. We live in a wanting world, and wherever we are, must expect to meet with something to put us out. It is a great mercy to have plenty of water, a mercy which, if we found the want of, we should more own the worth of. Hereupon they murmured against Moses and Aaron. They spake the same absurd and brutish language their fathers had done. It made their crime the worse, that they had smarted so long for the discontent and distrusts of their fathers, yet they venture in the same steps. Moses must again, in God's name, command water out of a rock for them; God is as able as ever to supply his people with what is needful for them. But Moses and Aaron acted wrong. They took much of the glory of this work of wonder to themselves; "Must we fetch water?" As if it were done by some power or worthiness of their own. They were to speak to the rock, but they smote it. Therefore it is charged upon them, that they did not sanctify God, that is, they did not give to him alone that glory of this miracle which was due unto his name. And being provoked by the people, Moses spake unadvisedly with his lips. The same pride of man would still usurp the office of the appointed Mediator; and become to ourselves wisdom, righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption. Such a state of sinful independence, such a rebellion of the soul against its Saviour, the voice of God condemns in every page of the gospel.
[Num.20.14-Num.20.21]
Verses 14-21
The nearest way to Canaan from the place where Israel encamped, was through the country of Edom. The ambassadors who were sent returned with a denial. The Edomites feared to receive damage by the Israelites. And had this numerous army been under any other discipline than that of the righteous God himself, there might have been cause for this jealousy. But Esau hated Jacob because of the blessing; and now the hatred revived, when the blessing was about to be inherited. We must not think it strange, if reasonable requests be denied by unreasonable men, and if those whom God favours be affronted by men.
[Num.20.22-Num.20.29]
Verses 22-29
God bids Aaron prepare to die. There is something of displeasure in these orders. Aaron must not enter Canaan, because he had failed in his duty at the waters of strife. There is much of mercy in them. Aaron, though he dies for his transgression, dies with ease, and in honour. He is gathered to his people, as one who dies in the arms of Divine grace. There is much significancy in these orders. Aaron must not enter Canaan, to show that the Levitical priesthood could make nothing perfect; that must be done by bringing in a better hope. Aaron submits, and dies in the method and manner appointed; and, for aught that appears, with as much cheerfulness as if he had been going to bed. It was a great satisfaction to Aaron to see his son, who was dear to him, preferred; and his office preserved and secured: especially, to see in this a figure of Christ's everlasting priesthood. A good man would desire, if it were the will of God, not to outlive his usefulness. Why should we covet to continue any longer in this world, than while we may do some service in it for God and our generation?
